meta.title: Send Files from iPhone to Android: 8 Ways That Work (2026)
meta.description: How to send photos, videos and files from an iPhone to an Android phone in 2026: AirDrop to Quick Share, iCloud links, Google Drive, USB-C and a free direct app.

hero.title: Send files from iPhone to Android
hero.body: Most guides on this still open with "AirDrop doesn't work with Android". That stopped being entirely true in late 2025, when Google taught Quick Share to speak AirDrop, and in early 2026 Apple added a Transfer to Android option to iOS. Both help, but each covers a narrower case than the headlines suggest. This page sorts out which of the eight real ways fits a single photo, a folder of video, a friend across town and a full phone switch, and where BIShare fills the gaps: any iPhone to any Android phone, straight across Wi-Fi or through a link. Open source, free to use, and nobody has to register.

updated: Updated September 2026 · Device list checked against Google's Quick Share page, migration steps against Apple's iOS 26.3 support article
disclosure: BIShare is ours. Several options below are built into the phones and cost nothing, and if the Android phone is on Google's supported list, AirDrop itself may be all you need; we say so where it applies.

quick.title: Quick answer
items: Android phone is a recent Pixel, Galaxy S or foldable: try AirDrop first. Set the iPhone to Everyone for 10 minutes, make the Android phone visible to everyone, and it appears in the AirDrop sheet.
Any other Android phone, same Wi-Fi: BIShare on both phones sends the original files directly and encrypted, with no size limit.
Nothing to install on the Android phone: send a link. A BIShare link carries up to 100 GB and opens in Chrome; an iCloud link does the same for photos and lasts 30 days.
One big video by email: Mail Drop in the iPhone's Mail app handles attachments up to 5 GB and works with a Gmail address.
Switching to Android for good: use Transfer to Android in iOS 26.3 or later with an Android 17 phone. It moves photos, messages, contacts and even the eSIM, which no file-sharing app does.
Don't bother with Bluetooth: an iPhone will not send files over Bluetooth to an Android phone, even when the two are paired.

changed.title: What changed in 2026, and what didn't
changed.body: Two changes from Apple and Google reshaped this question in the space of a few months. Neither turns every iPhone and Android pair into a one-tap handoff, so it helps to know exactly where each one reaches.

0.h: AirDrop can now reach some Android phones
0.b: <goAirdropAndroid>Google made Quick Share interoperable with AirDrop</goAirdropAndroid>, starting with the Pixel 10 in November 2025. Pixel 9 models and the 8a followed, then Samsung flagships (Galaxy S24, S25, S26, and the sixth and seventh generation Fold and Flip once updated to One UI 8.5). By June 2026 the list also named the OnePlus 15, Xiaomi 17T Pro, Honor Magic V6, Oppo's Find N6 and Find X9 range, and Vivo's X300 range. Every iPhone can take part. A mid-range Galaxy A, an older Pixel or most budget phones cannot.

1.b: iOS 26.3 added Transfer to Android under Settings, General, Transfer or Reset iPhone. It pairs with a phone running Android 17 by QR code and moves photos, contacts, calendars, call history and messages, and on supported carriers the eSIM number too. It is built for leaving the iPhone, not for handing one file to a friend who keeps theirs.

2.b: A built-in way to send a file to an Android phone that is not on Google's list. <goTransfer>A built-in way to reach an Android phone that is not in the same room</goTransfer>. And any Bluetooth file transfer from an iPhone at all. Those three are why the rest of this page exists.

0.name: BIShare
0.tag: Best overall: works with every Android phone, near or far
0.facts: Apps for iOS and Android, also desktop · MIT-licensed, costs nothing · uncapped between phones on one network · links hold 100 GB · encrypted end to end · sign-up not needed
0.body: The phone model does not matter. With the app on both phones and both on one Wi-Fi, the Android phone shows up in the iPhone's device list, you pick it, the other person taps accept, and the originals travel straight across at the speed of your network without touching a server. Photos keep their full resolution and videos are not re-encoded. When the other person is somewhere else, or would rather not install anything, the app switches to a shareable link (with a QR code and a short 6-character code as alternatives); the recipient opens that in Chrome, Samsung Internet or whatever browser the phone has, and pulls down as much as 100 GB. The file is encrypted on the iPhone before it uploads and the link expires after 24 hours.
0.cons: The direct Wi-Fi route needs the app on the Android phone as well. Links are meant for handing files over, not for keeping them, so the file is gone once the link expires.

1.name: AirDrop to Quick Share
1.tag: Best built-in option, if the Android phone is on the list
1.facts: Every iPhone · Pixel 10, 9, 8a, Galaxy S24–S26, Z Fold/Flip 6 and 7, selected Xiaomi, OnePlus, Oppo, Vivo, Honor · nearby only · no app · no size limit published
1.body: On a supported phone this is the closest thing to AirDrop between two iPhones. Open Control Center on the iPhone, set AirDrop to Everyone for 10 minutes, and make the Android phone visible to everyone in its Quick Share settings. On a Samsung phone, also turn on Share with Apple devices. The Android phone then appears in the iPhone's share sheet like any Apple device, and it works the other way round too. Both phones need Bluetooth and Wi-Fi switched on and have to be within a few metres of each other.
1.cons: Contacts Only mode cannot work across the two platforms, so both sides must be open to everyone nearby while you send. And the list of supported phones leaves out most Android phones in use today.

2.name: An iCloud link or Mail Drop
2.tag: Built into the iPhone, opens in any browser
2.facts: Every iPhone · iCloud link for photos and videos, expires after 30 days · Mail Drop up to 5 GB, expires after 30 days · needs iCloud on the sender's side
2.body: Two Apple features are easy to miss. In Photos, select pictures or videos, tap Share and choose Copy iCloud Link; the link opens in a browser on the Android phone and stays live for 30 days. For files rather than photos, attach them in the Mail app and send to the Android owner's Gmail address. Anything too big for a normal attachment is offered as Mail Drop, which carries up to 5 GB and does not count against your iCloud storage.
2.cons: Everything goes through Apple's servers at your upload speed. iCloud links need iCloud Photos turned on, and Mail Drop links stop working after 30 days.

3.name: Google Drive or Google Photos
3.tag: Best when the files should stay in the cloud
3.facts: Apps on iPhone, preinstalled on most Android phones · 15 GB free, shared across Gmail, Drive and Photos · Google account required
3.body: Most Android owners already have a Google account and the Photos and Drive apps. Upload from the iPhone, then share the album or file with their address, or send a link. It suits a shared family album that keeps growing, or a folder both of you will return to. In Google Photos, check that backup quality is set to Original if you care about full resolution.
3.cons: It is an upload followed by a download, so it is slow for large video, it eats into a 15 GB free allowance, and you need a Google account on the iPhone.

4.name: LocalSend
4.tag: Open-source app for the same Wi-Fi
4.facts: iOS, Android and desktop apps · open source, free · local network only · encrypted · nobody signs up
4.body: <goLocalsend>LocalSend</goLocalsend> does the same-network part of what BIShare does, and does it well: install it on both phones, they find each other, and files go across directly. For two people in one house who only ever swap files in person, it is a solid free choice.
4.cons: It cannot hand a file to a phone somewhere else, and it is no help if the other person won't install anything.

5.name: WhatsApp or Telegram, sent as a document
5.tag: Fine when the chat already exists
5.facts: Both phones need the app and an account · documents up to 2 GB · photos sent the normal way are compressed
5.body: If you already talk in WhatsApp or Telegram, this is the path of least effort. The trick is how you attach. A photo sent through the gallery picker is shrunk and recompressed; the same photo attached as a document keeps its original size and quality. In WhatsApp, tap the attachment button, choose Document and pick the file from Files or Photos.
5.cons: A 2 GB ceiling per file, a copy sitting in the chat history, and it is easy to forget the document trick and send a blurry version.

6.name: A USB-C flash drive
6.tag: No network at all, for iPhone 15 and later
6.facts: iPhone 15 or later with USB-C · Android phone with USB-C · exFAT drive · Files app on both
6.body: An iPhone with a USB-C port reads and writes external drives in the Files app, and it can format them there too. Copy the files onto the drive, plug it into the Android phone and open its Files app. Format the drive as exFAT so single files over 4 GB fit. Most current Android phones read exFAT, and Pixels have since Android 13; if yours does not, FAT32 works everywhere but refuses any file of 4 GB or more.
6.cons: You need the drive in hand, iPhones with a Lightning port need an adapter that not every drive supports, and copying photos out of the Photos app to Files first is an extra step.

7.name: A computer in the middle
7.facts: Windows PC or Mac · two cables · no internet needed · slow to set up
7.body: Plug the iPhone into a Windows PC, copy photos from its DCIM folder in File Explorer, then plug in the Android phone and paste them into its storage. On a Mac, import with the Photos app and copy to the Android phone through a file manager app.
7.cons: Two cables, a computer, trust prompts on both phones, and on a Mac an extra app just to see Android storage. Worth it only when nothing else is available.

switching.title: Moving everything to a new Android phone
switching.body: <blogIosAndroid>Sending some files and switching phones are different jobs</blogIosAndroid>. If the Android phone is replacing the iPhone, use a migration tool rather than dragging files across one batch at a time.

0.h: Transfer to Android, built into iOS 26.3
0.b: The iPhone needs iOS 26.3 or later and the Android phone Android 17. Start setting up the Android phone, or on the iPhone go to Settings, General, Transfer or Reset iPhone, Transfer to Android. Keep the phones close with Bluetooth on, scan the QR code on the Android screen with the iPhone's camera, choose what to bring, and confirm. Photos, contacts, calendars, call history and messages move, along with accessibility settings, Home Screen layout and wallpaper.

1.h: The eSIM can come too, on some carriers
1.b: Apple lists AT&T, FirstNet, T-Mobile and Verizon in the US, KDDI in Japan, Deutsche Telekom in Germany, SFR in France and EE in the UK. Once the number moves, it stops working on the iPhone. Health data is not part of the transfer, and third-party app data only comes along if the developer has added support.

2.b: A phone that is not on Android 17 yet still has Google's own setup-time migration, which copies contacts, calendar events, photos and videos from the iPhone. It does not move the eSIM, so for anything outside what a migration tool carries, such as documents in the Files app, a file-sharing method from the list above fills in afterwards.

steps.title: iPhone to Android with BIShare, step by step

0.h: Install on both phones and join one Wi-Fi
0.b: Get BIShare from the App Store on the iPhone and from Google Play on the Android phone, then connect both to the same Wi-Fi. When iOS asks whether BIShare may find devices on your local network, allow it, or the Android phone will never appear. A phone hotspot works as the shared network if there is no Wi-Fi around.

1.h: Pick the files and the phone
1.b: Tap send, choose photos, videos or anything from Files, and select the Android phone from the list. The other person accepts, and the files land in their gallery or Downloads folder at full quality, encrypted on the way.

2.b: Not in the same place, or the Android owner does not want the app? Choose the link option, or open bishare.app/transfer in Safari and drop the files in. Send the link or 6-character code by any message; it opens in the Android phone's browser, downloads up to 100 GB, and expires after 24 hours.

photos.title: Why photos sometimes look wrong on Android, and how to avoid it
photos.body: Photo quality problems between iPhone and Android usually come from formats and compression rather than from the transfer itself.

0.b: iPhones save photos as HEIC by default. Android has decoded HEIC since Android 8.0 and Google Photos opens it, but some older gallery apps, editors and websites still refuse it. If the person receiving needs JPEG, switch the iPhone to Settings, Camera, Formats, Most Compatible before taking the photos.

1.b: A Live Photo is a still image with a short video attached, and Android has no format that plays the two together. Expect the still to arrive. If the moment matters, open the Live Photo, tap Share and choose Save as Video, then send that video.

2.b: Messaging apps resize and recompress photos and videos sent the normal way, which is why <blogPhotos>a crisp iPhone shot can arrive soft</blogPhotos>. Send the original file through a direct transfer, a link, or as a document.

3.b: iPhone video is usually HEVC, which Android has played since Android 5.0, so nearly every phone handles it. <goLargeFiles>Very large 4K or ProRes clips</goLargeFiles> are where transfer choice matters most: a direct Wi-Fi route moves them in seconds to minutes, while a cloud route has to upload the whole file first.

speed.title: How long a transfer takes
speed.body: Phones in the same room are limited by the Wi-Fi, not by the app. Anything that goes through the internet is limited by your upload speed.

0.b: With both phones close to a Wi-Fi 5 router, expect somewhere near 40–50 MB/s; a Wi-Fi 6 router lifts that to roughly 70–110 MB/s. A 1 GB video takes well under half a minute. <goOffline>Over a phone hotspot</goOffline>, expect roughly 10–30 MB/s.

1.b: The two phones build their own short-range connection, so a slow or absent router is not an obstacle. It suits a handful of photos or a few videos; for a large batch, keep both screens awake and the phones close together.

2.h: Links, iCloud, Drive and chat apps
2.b: The file uploads once and downloads once. On a 50 Mbps upload, 1 GB needs about three minutes before the Android phone can start downloading, and 10 GB takes more than half an hour.

fixes.title: When the Android phone doesn't show up

0.h: The Android phone isn't in the AirDrop sheet
0.b: Check it is on the supported list and up to date, that the iPhone is <goAirdropFix>set to Everyone for 10 minutes rather than Contacts Only</goAirdropFix>, that the Android phone is visible to everyone, and on Samsung that Share with Apple devices is on. Both need Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on and the screens unlocked.

1.h: The phones share a Wi-Fi but can't see each other in an app
1.b: On the iPhone, open Settings, Privacy & Security, Local Network and make sure the app is allowed. Guest networks and some office or hotel Wi-Fi keep devices apart; use a phone hotspot instead. A VPN on either phone can also block local discovery.

2.b: That is expected. <goAirdropAlt>iPhones only exchange files with other Apple devices</goAirdropAlt>, so pairing with an Android phone over Bluetooth never offers file transfer. Use Wi-Fi or a link.

3.h: Photos won't open on the Android phone
3.b: They are almost certainly HEIC and the app in use cannot read them. Open them in Google Photos, or resend from an iPhone set to Most Compatible, which saves new photos as JPEG.

4.b: Link speed is capped by the sender's upload. If both phones are actually in the same place, switch to a direct Wi-Fi route, which skips the internet entirely.

security.title: Who can see the files on the way
security.body: Photos of family, ID scans and documents deserve a route that does not leave copies behind. This is how the options compare.

0.b: BIShare's direct route, LocalSend and AirDrop to Quick Share send between the two phones and encrypt the connection. No copy is left on a server.

1.h: Through a server that cannot read it
1.b: <goEncrypted>BIShare links encrypt the file on the iPhone before upload</goEncrypted> and put the decryption key after the # in the address. Browsers do not transmit that fragment, so the server only ever stores scrambled data. WhatsApp documents are end-to-end encrypted too, but stay in both chat histories.

2.b: iCloud links, Mail Drop and Google Drive encrypt files in transit and on their servers, but under standard settings the provider holds the keys. Fine for holiday photos, worth a second thought for passports and contracts.

0.q: Can you AirDrop from an iPhone to an Android phone?
0.a: Yes, if the Android phone supports Quick Share's AirDrop compatibility: the Pixel 10, 9 and 8a, the Galaxy S24, S25 and S26 lines and the Z Fold/Flip 6 and 7, plus selected Xiaomi, OnePlus, Oppo, Vivo and Honor models. Set the iPhone's AirDrop to Everyone for 10 minutes. Other Android phones cannot receive AirDrop.

1.q: What is the easiest way to send files from iPhone to Android?
1.a: If the Android phone is on Google's supported list, AirDrop with both sides visible to everyone. Otherwise, install BIShare on both and send over the same Wi-Fi, or send a BIShare link that opens in the Android phone's browser.

2.q: Can I send files from iPhone to Android via Bluetooth?
2.a: No. iPhones do not transfer files over Bluetooth to non-Apple devices, even when paired. Use a Wi-Fi app, AirDrop to a supported Android phone, or a link.

3.q: How do I keep full photo quality when sending from iPhone to Android?
3.a: Send the original files by a direct transfer, a BIShare or iCloud link, Google Drive, or as a document in WhatsApp. Avoid attaching them as normal photos in chat apps, which compresses them. If the recipient needs JPEG, set the iPhone to Most Compatible.

4.q: How do I send a large video from iPhone to Android?
4.a: On the same Wi-Fi, a direct app such as BIShare has no size limit. Apart, a BIShare link carries up to 100 GB and Mail Drop up to 5 GB. WhatsApp documents stop at 2 GB.

5.q: Can I send files from iPhone to Android without an app?
5.a: Yes. Use Copy iCloud Link in Photos, Mail Drop in the Mail app, or bishare.app/transfer in Safari; the Android phone opens each in a browser. A supported Android phone can also receive AirDrop directly.

6.q: Does iOS 26.3 let me transfer to Android?
6.a: Yes, for switching phones. Transfer to Android in Settings moves photos, messages, contacts, calendars and call history to a phone running Android 17, and the eSIM on supported carriers. It is not meant for sending a single file.

7.q: Why can't my Android phone open photos from my iPhone?
7.a: They are probably HEIC. Android can decode HEIC and Google Photos opens it, but some apps cannot. Set the iPhone's camera format to Most Compatible to save future photos as JPEG.

8.q: Must the iPhone and the Android phone share a Wi-Fi network?
8.a: Only for direct routes, meaning BIShare phone to phone or LocalSend. AirDrop to Quick Share needs the phones close together with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on. Links, iCloud, Drive and chat apps work anywhere.

9.q: Is it free to send files from iPhone to Android?
9.a: Yes. BIShare, LocalSend, AirDrop to Quick Share, iCloud links, Mail Drop and Google Drive's free 15 GB all cost nothing. Only very large or long-term cloud storage needs a paid plan.

cta.title: Every iPhone, every Android phone
cta.body: No cost, no sign-up, code on GitHub. Beam files across the room over Wi-Fi, or across the country with a link that opens in the Android phone's browser.
